questions.question_text: What is the definition of $1\text{ radian}$?

options.text: The angle subtended at the centre of a circle by an arc whose length equals the radius.
The angle subtended at the centre of a circle by an arc equal to the diameter.
options.why: Used the diameter of the circle instead of the radius in the definition.

options.text: The angle subtended at the centre by an arc of length $1\text{ cm}$ in any circle.
options.why: Treated $1\text{ radian}$ as a fixed metric arc length regardless of radius.

options.text: The fraction of a circle obtained by dividing $360^{\circ}$ by $100$.
options.why: Confused radians with gradian measure ($100$ gradians per right angle).

questions.solution_text: One radian is the angle subtended at the centre of a circle when the arc length equals the radius ($l = r$).

questions.question_text: Why does one complete revolution ($360^{\circ}$) equal $2\pi\text{ radians}$?

options.text: Because the full circumference is $2\pi r$, and dividing arc length by radius gives $\dfrac{2\pi r}{r} = 2\pi$.
Because $\pi$ is defined as $180^{\circ}$, so doubling it gives $360^{\circ}$.
options.why: Cited the conversion consequence rather than the geometric derivation from circumference.

options.text: Because a circle has two semicircles of radius $\pi$.
options.why: Confused the angle $\pi$ radians with a physical radius length of $\pi$.

options.text: Because the area of a unit circle is $\pi r^2$, which doubles to $2\pi$.
options.why: Confused circumference and angular subtension with circle area.

questions.solution_text:
One full revolution subtends the full circumference $C = 2\pi r$.
$\theta = \dfrac{\text{arc length}}{\text{radius}} = \dfrac{2\pi r}{r} = 2\pi\text{ radians}$

questions.question_text:
An arc of length $18\text{ cm}$ subtends an angle $\theta$ at the centre of a circle of radius $6\text{ cm}$.
What is the value of $\theta$ in radians?

options.why: Multiplied arc length by radius instead of dividing arc length by radius.
Divided radius by arc length instead of arc length by radius.
Appended $\pi$ to the numeric value when $\pi$ was not present in the lengths.

questions.question_text: If a central angle in a circle of radius $r$ is $3.5\text{ radians}$, what is the length of the subtended arc?

options.why: Divided the angle by the radius instead of multiplying.
Inverted the relationship between arc length and radius.
Multiplied by $\pi$ unnecessarily when the angle is already given in radians.

questions.question_text:
An arc of a circle subtends $\dfrac{1}{6}$ of a full revolution at the centre.
What is the central angle in radians?

options.why: Multiplied by $\pi$ instead of the full revolution $2\pi$.
Multiplied by $4\pi$ instead of $2\pi$.
Converted $\frac{1}{6}$ of $360^{\circ}$ to $60$ and multiplied by $\pi$.

questions.solution_text:
One full revolution is $2\pi\text{ radians}$.
$\theta = \dfrac{1}{6} \times 2\pi$
$= \dfrac{\pi}{3}\text{ radians}$

questions.question_text: Why is radian measure considered a dimensionless unit?

options.text: It is the ratio of two lengths (arc length and radius), so the units cancel out.
It is based on the irrational number $\pi$, which has no physical units.
options.why: Attributed dimensionless nature to irrationality rather than the ratio of lengths.

options.text: Angles cannot be measured with physical instruments like rulers or calipers.
options.why: Made an incorrect assertion about physical measurement tools.

options.text: It was defined to have no units so that it matches degrees.
options.why: Degrees are an arbitrary scale unit, whereas radians are naturally dimensionless.

questions.solution_text: Radian measure is defined as $\theta = \dfrac{l}{r}$. Both $l$ and $r$ are measured in the same units of length, which cancel in the quotient.

questions.question_text:
An arc of length $5\pi\text{ cm}$ is part of a circle with radius $10\text{ cm}$.
What is the central angle in radians?

options.why: Divided the radius by the arc length instead of arc length by radius.
Multiplied the arc length by the radius.
Dropped $\pi$ from the numerator during the division.

questions.question_text:
In a circle of radius $r$, an arc has length equal to the diameter $2r$.
What central angle does this arc subtend, and what fraction of a full circle is it?

options.why: Assumed an arc equal to the diameter sweeps the entire circumference.
Treated the arc length as $1$ radius rather than $2$ radii.
Doubled the angle calculation incorrectly.

questions.question_text:
A circular track has radius $50\text{ m}$.
A runner completes an arc of length $100\pi\text{ m}$.
How many complete revolutions does this run represent?

options.why: Used $C = pi r$ instead of $C = 2pi r$ for the circumference of one revolution.
Doubled the required track circumference.
Divided the arc length by $pi$ and subtracted the radius.

questions.solution_text:
Circumference of track:
$C = 2\pi r = 2\pi \times 50 = 100\pi\text{ m}$
Since the distance is $100\pi\text{ m}$, the runner completes exactly $1\text{ revolution}$ ($2\pi\text{ radians}$).
